_comment: GENERATED by scripts/analytics/catalogue.mjs from spa/src/analytics/catalogue/ and scripts/serve/probes.py. Do not hand-edit: `make analytics-catalogue-check` compares this byte for byte with what those two sources render right now.

app.page.viewed.what: a route transition committed — the visitor is now looking at a different page

boot.index.fetch.what: the boot-video index was fetched and merged onto the catalog

boot.video.played.what: a boot video actually started playing in front of somebody

fleet.faceted.what: a human filtered the fleet table by a column facet

fleet.searched.what: a human typed in the fleet free-text filter

fleet.sorted.what: a human sorted the fleet table by some column

fleet.usage.fetch.what: the per-station interaction totals were fetched from the server

fleet.usage.shown.what: at least one row rendered with real usage numbers in it, in a visible tab

fleet.usage.sorted.what: a human sorted the fleet BY the usage column — the strongest evidence the fetch earns its keep

hall.entered.what: the 3D hall was mounted in front of somebody, in a visible tab

keyboard.osk.used.what: a key was pressed on the ON-SCREEN keyboard, not a physical one

station.key.used.what: a key went down on a live guest

station.pointer.used.what: a button went down on a live guest

stream.overlay.shown.what: the Cmd/Ctrl+N diagnostic overlay was actually on screen

stream.stats.polled.what: a station session started polling live stream stats for the debug overlay

walkin.play.claimInstant.what: a claim was answered with a clone immediately — the pool had a free machine for this visitor

walkin.play.claimQueued.what: a claim was answered with a queue position — every clone of that station was taken at that moment

walkin.register.refused.what: a stranger reached the walk-in door while access was closed and was shown the closed sentence

fleet.find.what: answering a question with the fleet table and leaving it by opening a machine

hall.navigate.what: entering the 3D hall and leaving it by opening a machine

keyboard.compose.what: typing something at a guest with the on-screen keyboard sheet

poster.read.what: opening an exhibit poster and reading it to the end

session.resume.what: a backgrounded tab or installed PWA coming back to a moving picture

station.connect.what: opening a station and getting a first frame out of it

stream.recover.what: a picture that stopped moving, and whether it started again before the visitor left

walkin.play.what: claiming a private clone and getting a machine the visitor actually drives

walkin.register.what: a stranger with no account getting one and reaching a machine to play

app.page.transitionMs.what: a high value means switching routes visibly hangs the app before the new view paints

fleet.find.actionsToStation.what: a high value means it takes many sorts and filters to isolate one machine — the default order and the column set are wrong for the questions people actually ask

fleet.find.hScrollReversals.what: a high value means people overshoot and backtrack — they cannot predict where a column is

fleet.find.hScrollScreens.what: a high value means the columns people want are far from the ones they land on

fleet.find.toFirstActionMs.what: a high value means people land on the table and cannot tell what to do with it — the controls do not suggest the first move

hall.navigate.stationsApproached.what: a high value means visitors stand in front of machine after machine without opening any — the placards are not telling people what they are looking at

hall.navigate.toFirstStationMs.what: a high value means the hall is scenery people wander rather than a way to reach a machine — spend the next hour on the grid instead

keyboard.compose.correctionsPct.what: a high value means this machine's hand-written key layout puts keys where people do not expect them, so the profile data is wrong and worth fixing before adding another

keyboard.compose.layerSwitches.what: a high value means the characters people need are spread across layers, so the split is costing more round trips than it saves screen space

keyboard.compose.toFirstKeyMs.what: a high value means the keyboard comes up and the key people came for is not findable at a glance, so the layout needs reordering rather than more keys

poster.read.dwellMs.what: a LOW value means posters are opened and dismissed unread — the prose is not earning the click, whatever it cost to write

poster.read.scrollDepthPct.what: a low value means people stop part way down — the essays are longer than the audience they are written for

poster.read.scrollReversals.what: a high value means people scroll back up mid-poster — a passage they had to read twice, and the first place to look when rewriting

session.resume.awayMs.what: a high value means visitors leave for longer than the idle-pause grace and wake lease assume, so those windows are tuned for a visit pattern that does not happen

session.resume.reconnectToLiveMs.what: a high value means rebuilding a dead session on resume is slow, so the fix is to keep sessions alive across a background rather than to reconnect faster

session.resume.toLiveMs.what: a high value means a session that survived being backgrounded still takes too long to start pulling again — the fix is in videoResume, not the transport

station.open.attemptCount.what: a high value means this station only connects by retrying, so its ladder is absorbing a fault nobody has been told about

station.open.toFirstFrameMs.what: a high value means visitors stare at a spinner between choosing a machine and seeing it

station.open.toFirstInputMs.what: a high value means visitors hesitate to touch this machine once it works — it needs a clearer invitation, not a faster stream

stream.recover.abandonedAfterMs.what: a low value means visitors abandon a frozen station quickly, so recovery must beat that budget or be replaced by an honest message — and the COUNT of these is how many visits the fleet is losing to freezes

stream.recover.stallMs.what: a high value means visitors sit through long visible freezes before the picture returns, so the recovery ladder is too slow to hide the fault it is recovering from

walkin.play.claimRetries.what: a high value means one press of Play does not get a machine, so the queue card is doing work the pool should be doing

walkin.play.queueMs.what: a high value means visitors who meet a full pool wait long enough to give up, which is the argument for raising poolSize past 3

walkin.play.toPlayableMs.what: a high value means the gap between being handed a clone and being able to use it is where walk-ins are lost, so the resume path is worth more than the claim path

walkin.register.exhibitPickMs.what: a high value means a visitor who already has an account still cannot choose between the three cards, so the cards are not telling the machines apart

walkin.register.hesitationMs.what: a high value means the walk-in page does not tell an arriving stranger what to do — rewrite the lede and the call to action before optimising anything downstream

walkin.register.landingMs.what: a high value means the landing page is where registrations stall, so shortening it beats speeding up anything after it

walkin.register.passkeyMs.what: a high value means the platform passkey ceremony is where the door spends its time, so the fix is preparing the visitor for it rather than changing our copy

walkin.register.passkeyRetries.what: a high value means passkey enrolment is failing for platform reasons visitors cannot fix, so the door needs a diagnosable failure path rather than better wording

auth.gate.blocked.what: something browser-reachable asked for the command ENQUEUE and was refused; a zero says the block is theoretical, and anything else is worth reading the access log over

auth.gate.invited.what: a signed-in NON-walk-in session was allowed through the public fence — the invited plane is in use

auth.gate.walkin.what: the walk-in allowlist was consulted for a real request — a stranger with an account is browsing

auth.gate.walkinOwn.what: a walk-in was allowed at their OWN clone's signaling or webrtc path — the one interactive surface the plane grants, so this is the plane being USED rather than merely reachable

clientlog.prune.age.what: the clientlog crossed its size backstop and the rolling age-prune actually dropped rows

clientlog.rotate.generational.what: the age-prune left the file STILL oversized and the single .1 generation rotate fired — i.e. the retention window is too wide for the disk budget. Suspected dead code; this is how that gets settled

signal.ticket.identityDiffers.what: a station's own signaling.json named an identity DIFFERENT from the endpoint key the document was fetched under, so the ticket was signed over the daemon's name and not the key. This exact divergence locked `solaris` and `aros` out of every session for four hours on 2026-08-05; a non-zero here means a station is mis-named RIGHT NOW and the fallback is the only thing hiding it

walkin.claim.queued.what: a claim found no free clone (or hit the active-session cap) and went into the QUEUE — a zero means the whole queue-and-position machinery has never once been needed

walkin.claim.resumeFailed.what: a clone was handed to a visitor and then would not resume, so `_abandon` ran; this is the path that keeps the 'a used clone is never re-listed' guarantee true under a failure

walkin.reap.died.what: the watchdog found a pool member whose QEMU had died and retired it; a non-zero here is a fleet health fact nothing else on the box reports

walkin.reap.idle.what: a session was ended by the 3-minute idle window — the reason code that decides whether the idle timer earns its keep, or is only ever beaten to it by the TTL

walkin.reap.ttl.what: a session was ended by the 20-minute clock
